title: Japji 1–7, whole
hook: the wall of falsehood, the order, the Giver, the early hours
tomorrow: four pauris in a row start with the same word. which one?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the same words, deeper: the Mool Mantar said slowly at the summit. Right after it, the Japji begins, and today its first stretch gets read in one go.
screen: `THE SAME WORDS, DEEPER.` → `NOW, THE JAPJI IN ONE GO.`

segments.voice: An email lands, and you read it once. Then again. Then a third time, hunting for the tone. By evening there are four drafted replies and none sent. Guru Nanak names this exact loop in the Japji's first pauri: sochai soch na hovaee je sochee lakh vaar. Think it over a hundred thousand times, and thinking still won't get you there. So what does?
screen: `ONE EMAIL, READ AGAIN AND AGAIN.` → `THINK A LAKH TIMES.` → `SO WHAT DOES GET YOU THERE?`

segments.voice: Read pauris one to seven in one sitting, and a single thread holds them: hukam, the order, the Will running through everything. Pauri one asks the question straight out: kiv sachiaaraa hoeeai, kiv koorrai tuttai paal. How do we become true? How does the wall of falsehood come down? Its last line answers: hukam rajaaee chalanaa. Walk in the order, the Will. Pauri two: everything is inside the order, nothing outside it. Pauri three: people sing of the Giver in endless ways, and the Giver keeps giving while the takers grow tired. Pauri four: the true Lord, and the early hours for the true Name. Pauri five: the One can't be installed or made, and the plea, may I not forget the one Giver of all. Pauri six: bathing at pilgrim places counts only if it pleases the One. Pauri seven: even a life four ages long, known in every land, means nothing without grace. Read whole, it works like a loosening. Overthinking, cleverness, ritual, fame: each one gets set down in turn. What's left isn't a technique. It's a direction.
screen: `ONE THREAD: HUKAM, THE ORDER.` · `HOW DOES THE WALL COME DOWN?` · `THE GIVER, THE EARLY HOURS.` · `EACH CLEVER ROUTE SET DOWN.` · then, large: `WALK IN THE ORDER.`

segments.voice: Open the Japji, in a gutka, an app or on a printed page, and read from pauri one onward at an easy pace, in Gurmukhi or English. Don't stop to study a line. When the sit ends, stop where you are, and let the last line you read be the one you keep.
Japji 1. The Japji's first seven pauris, read whole: one thread, the order, from the wall of falsehood to the early hours and the one Giver.
Something to keep: walk in the order, which no amount of thinking can replace. Two of the summit.

screen: `DAY 1762 COUNTS.` → `THE SUMMIT · 2 OF 31.` → `TOMORROW: FOUR PAURIS IN A ROW START WITH THE SAME WORD. WHICH ONE?`

howItsDone: Sikhs who keep nitnem recite the whole Japji in the morning as the first of the daily banis, from a gutka or from memory, reading straight through from pauri to pauri.

fork.setup: a friend tries a day of total silence to feel closer to God, and feels nothing. what does pauri one say about that?
options: silence alone, like thinking alone, won't do it; pauri one points to walking in the Will.
she should keep it up longer; pauri one says effort builds until it works.
the Japji forbids silent practice, so she should drop it entirely.
fork.reveal: pauri one names thinking, silence, appetite and cleverness, and says none alone gets you there. its answer is hukam rajaaee chalanaa: walk in the order.

original.note: Gurmukhi: by the order, the Will, the thread through the Japji's first pauris.

trapdoor: what you thought: seven separate verses to memorize.
what it means: one thread, the order, running through them all and loosening every clever route.
what a scholar hears: pauri one's question, kiv sachiaaraa hoeeai, is answered by its own last line, hukam rajaaee chalanaa, and pauri two carries the word on.

chat.says: college housing email came. reread it all night looking for a hidden problem. how do i stop??
options: Pauri one: thinking a lakh times won't get you there. Do the next step, then trust the order.
Read it once more, slowly; Guru Nanak says deep thought is how truth comes.
Ignore it completely; the Japji says nothing you do changes anything.
chat.meaning: The Japji's first pauri says thinking a lakh times won't bring you there. Its answer is a direction: walk in the order, the Will.

Japji.meaning: Guru Nanak's morning hymn that opens the Guru Granth Sahib

pauri.meaning: a stanza; the word also means a step on a stair

hukam.meaning: the order, the divine Will running through everything

Pauri summaries (paraphrased): 2 all within hukam; 3 the Giver gives and takers tire (dendaa de lainde thak paahi); 4 the true Lord, amrit vela; 5 thaapiaa na jaae, and sabhnaa jeeaa kaa ik daataa so mai visar na jaaee; 6 teerath naavaa je tis bhaavaa; 7 je jug chaare aarjaa. Confirm each. 'A hundred thousand' is the meaning of lakh in the quoted line; 'four ages' is the text's chaare jug.
